chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Market Cycles, Era by Era

body.text: Between 2003 and 2008 almost every cycle from Chapter 1 turned up at once in India: investment, credit, real estate, global commodities and foreign capital. The Sensex rose about seven times in under five years. When they all turned down together, it lost almost two thirds in ten months.

children.text: Lesson 3.2 ended in April 2003 with the Sensex near 2,900, retail investors burned, and scams in the headlines. Nobody called it the start of a supercycle. This lesson covers the up leg of India's biggest bull market to date: why it happened, how much of it came from real growth versus rising valuations, and the warning signs that were visible in late 2007 and early 2008. The crash itself and its global causes are a story of their own. The focus here is the anatomy of the whole cycle.

stats.label: Sensex, October 2008
stats.context: Intraday low, about 64% below the peak

children.text: Remember Schumpeter's idea from Lesson 1.2: the biggest booms come when several cycles rise at the same time. In 2003 an unusual number of engines were all at or near their lows, and all started turning up within a year or two of each other.

body.caption: The engines of the 2003 to 2008 boom

cells: Reforms bearing fruit
A decade of 1990s reforms, new telecom and IT industries, stronger exchanges and depositories, and cleaned-up company balance sheets after years of caution
The repair phase of the credit cycle, Lesson 1.3
Low interest rates
Rates in India were at multi-decade lows in 2003 to 2004, making home loans and business borrowing cheap
Credit cycle, expansion stage
Corporate investment
Companies built power plants, steel mills, roads, ports and telecom networks at a record pace
Juglar investment cycle, Lesson 1.2
Real estate
Housing and commercial property prices and construction surged across major cities
Kuznets building cycle, Lesson 1.2
Global liquidity and commodities
Low US interest rates, China's rapid growth and a worldwide commodity boom sent money flooding into emerging markets
Global credit and commodity cycles, Chapter 4
Foreign capital
Foreign institutional investors poured money into Indian shares, with net inflows of roughly $17 billion in 2007 alone
The flows that the 1992 reforms made possible, Lesson 3.2

body.text: None of these engines was imaginary. India's economy genuinely grew faster in this period than at almost any time since independence, and many companies built real, lasting businesses. That is exactly what makes a supercycle dangerous: the story is true, so investors stop asking what price the truth is worth.

children.text: Not a Straight Line, Even Then

body.title: Sensex at major turning points, 2003 to 2009 (approximate intraday levels)

cells: January to May 2004
~31%, including a fall of more than 15% intraday on 17 May 2004
Surprise election result and fears about reform policy under a new coalition government
Reforms continued, and the Sensex made a new high within about a year
May to June 2006
~29% in about five weeks
Global sell-off in emerging markets as US rates rose, after a steep run-up
The Sensex recovered its peak within about six months and went on to 20,000
January 2008 onwards
~31% by March 2008, ~64% by October 2008
US subprime crisis, record oil prices, rate hikes, FII selling and finally the Lehman collapse
A full bear market. The Sensex did not close above its January 2008 high until November 2010

children.text: Here is the trap. Twice during the boom, the market fell about 30%, and twice it bounced back to new highs within months. Every investor who bought those dips was rewarded, and the lesson got stronger each time: falls are buying opportunities. So when the Sensex fell about 31% between January and March 2008, many treated it the same way. This time the engines underneath had turned. The same behaviour that worked in 2004 and 2006 was exactly the wrong response in 2008, the pattern Lesson 2.3 warned about.

body.title: The Speed of the Boom
body.prompt: The Sensex rose from about 2,900 in April 2003 to about 21,200 in January 2008, a period of about 4.7 years. What was its CAGR over that period, before dividends? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: Multiple = 21,200 ÷ 2,900 ≈ 7.31. CAGR = 7.31 to the power 1/4.7, minus 1 ≈ 1.527 − 1 ≈ 53% a year. For comparison, the Sensex's long-run average from Lesson 1.1 is about 16% a year. A pace more than three times the long-run average cannot continue indefinitely, and usually signals that valuations as well as earnings are rising fast.

children.text: Earnings or Euphoria? Splitting the Gain

Use the split from Lessons 1.1 and 2.3 once more: price growth equals earnings growth multiplied by the change in P/E. In early 2003 the main Indian indices traded at a trailing P/E of roughly 12. By January 2008 the Nifty's P/E was around 28. The multiple had more than doubled, which tells you a large share of the rise came from investors paying more for each rupee of profit, not just from profits growing.

body.title: Split the Supercycle
body.question: The Sensex rose about 7.3 times between 2003 and 2008, while the market P/E rose from about 12 to about 28. Roughly how many times did underlying earnings grow?
options: About 7.3 times, the same as the index
Earnings did not grow at all
body.explanation: The P/E multiple grew by 28 ÷ 12 ≈ 2.33 times. Price growth = earnings growth × P/E growth, so earnings growth ≈ 7.3 ÷ 2.33 ≈ 3.1 times. Tripling earnings in five years is an outstanding result. But more than a third of the gain in multiplicative terms came from a higher P/E, and that part could reverse quickly, which is what happened in 2008, when the P/E fell back toward its 2003 level.

events.title: The RBI tightens
events.description: With inflation rising and credit growing fast, the RBI raises its repo rate and bank cash reserve requirements repeatedly, and increases capital requirements on lending to real estate. The credit cycle is moving from expansion to excess.

events.title: A record real estate IPO
events.description: DLF raises about ₹9,200 crore, then the largest IPO in Indian history. Property developers, many heavily borrowed, become some of the most valuable companies on the market.

events.title: The decoupling story
events.description: As the US subprime crisis unfolds, a popular theory holds that India and other emerging markets have decoupled from the US and will keep growing regardless. The rupee strengthens to around 39 per dollar, and FII inflows hit a record.

events.title: Sensex closes above 20,000
events.description: The index has roughly doubled in about 18 months. Power, infrastructure, real estate and capital goods stocks lead, many trading at extreme valuations on projected rather than current earnings.

events.title: The peak and the frenzy
events.description: The Sensex hits about 21,200. Reliance Power's IPO of about ₹11,560 crore draws bids worth roughly 70 times the shares on offer, with heavy retail participation. Days later the market begins to fall sharply.

events.title: A telling listing
events.description: Reliance Power lists on 11 February and closes its first day at around ₹372, about 17% below its issue price of ₹450, a clear signal that the euphoria stage was over.

events.title: Every engine reverses
events.description: Crude oil peaks near $147 a barrel in July, Indian inflation climbs into double digits, the RBI raises the repo rate to 9%, FIIs pull out roughly $13 billion over the year, and Lehman Brothers collapses in September. The Sensex falls to about 7,700 in October.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: In January 2008, the IPO of ___ drew bids worth roughly 70 times the shares on offer, then listed about 17% below its issue price in February.
body.explanation: A record-breaking IPO frenzy followed by a weak listing is one of the most reliable late-cycle signals. It shows demand driven by recent gains rather than value, and the moment that demand is no longer enough to push prices higher.

body.title: The India story vs the cycle, early 2008

columns.label: What was true about India
points: GDP growth above 9% for three years
A young population and rising incomes
Far stronger market institutions than in the 1990s
Long-term prospects that did prove strong

columns.label: What was also true about the cycle
points: Market P/E more than double its 2003 level
Rising inflation and repeated rate hikes
Heavy dependence on foreign money that could leave quickly
Heavily borrowed developers and infrastructure firms leading the market
Record IPOs, record retail participation and a decoupling story

body.text: The most expensive stocks of 2007 were not the ones that fell least. Real estate, power and infrastructure favourites led the boom on borrowed money and projected earnings, and many fell 80% to 90% or more once credit tightened. Some, such as Unitech, never recovered and later ended up in legal proceedings. Others spent more than a decade below their 2008 prices. The Nifty 50 recovered. Many of the stocks that led it up did not.

body.title: The Reliance Power Decision
body.scenario: It is January 2008. Your father, a government employee in Lucknow, has ₹3 lakh in fixed deposits. His colleagues are all applying to the Reliance Power IPO, the Sensex has crossed 20,000, and a financial channel says India has decoupled from the US slowdown. He plans to break his FDs, apply for the maximum retail amount, and use any listing gains to buy real estate and infrastructure stocks.
body.prompt: Using what you learned in this lesson and this course, what signals would you point out, and what would you suggest instead?
body.modelAnswer: Nearly every late-cycle signal from this course is present. The Sensex has risen about seven times in under five years, a pace of about 53% a year, far above its long-run average. Market valuations are more than double their 2003 level. A record IPO is heavily oversubscribed, with colleagues applying because everyone else is, which is Kindleberger's euphoria stage. There is a popular theory explaining why the usual risks do not apply this time, the decoupling story. The RBI has been raising rates and inflation is rising, so the credit cycle is late. And the plan concentrates everything in the most cyclical, most borrowed sectors of the boom, funded by breaking safe deposits. None of this means anyone could have predicted the exact top or the Lehman collapse. But the cycle-aware response is not to go all in at the moment when every engine is stretched. A better approach would be to keep his emergency and near-term money in FDs, invest any long-term surplus gradually through an SIP in a diversified index fund rather than a lump sum, and avoid building a portfolio around the hottest sectors and listing-day gains. In fact, the IPO listed below its issue price, and the sectors he planned to buy fell far more than the index.

cards.definition: An unusually long and powerful boom in which several economic and market cycles rise together, such as India's investment, credit, real estate, commodity and foreign capital cycles from 2003 to 2008.
Net purchases or sales of Indian securities by foreign institutional investors, now called foreign portfolio investors. Record inflows in 2007 reversed to heavy outflows in 2008.
The 2007 to 2008 belief that emerging markets like India could keep growing unaffected by a US slowdown. The 2008 crash disproved it for markets.
The habit formed when several sharp falls recover quickly, as in 2004 and 2006, which leads investors to treat the start of a real bear market as another opportunity.
Record-sized, heavily oversubscribed IPOs in the hottest sectors, especially followed by weak listings, as with DLF in 2007 and Reliance Power in 2008.
The market P/E rose from about 12 to about 28, so earnings grew about three times while prices rose about seven times.

body.label: NSDL: FPI Monitor
body.description: NSDL publishes daily, monthly and yearly data on net investment by foreign portfolio investors in Indian equity and debt. Look at the calendar year totals for 2007 and 2008 to see how quickly foreign money can reverse.

children.text: After the 2008 crash, the Nifty 50 recovered sharply in 2009. The cycles underneath it did not. Lesson 3.4 covers the long grind from 2009 to 2014, when stalled projects, bad loans, inflation and policy paralysis kept Indian markets going sideways while other markets moved on.

body.text: Index levels, valuation multiples, flows and IPO figures in this lesson are approximate and rounded. References to specific companies describe widely reported historical events for educational purposes only, and are not recommendations to buy or sell any security or investment advice.

points: From April 2003 to January 2008 the Sensex rose from about 2,900 to about 21,200, roughly 7.3 times, or about 53% a year
The boom was powered by several cycles turning up together: reforms bearing fruit, low rates, record corporate investment, real estate, global liquidity and record FII inflows
Earnings grew about three times, but the market P/E also rose from about 12 to about 28, so a large part of the gain came from higher valuations
Falls of about 30% in 2004 and 2006 recovered quickly, which conditioned investors to buy the dip when the real bear market began in 2008
Late-cycle signals included rising inflation and rate hikes, record IPOs like DLF and Reliance Power, a decoupling story and leadership by heavily borrowed sectors
When the engines reversed together, the Sensex fell about 64% by October 2008, and many of the boom's leading stocks never regained their peaks
